title: Crochet decrease basics
subtitle: Work two stitches as one so the fabric loses a stitch in width
excerpt: A crochet decrease takes two stitches at the base and works them as a single stitch at the top. The row loses one stitch in width. The shaping move every beanie crown, sleeve cap, and amigurumi closing uses.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet shaping fundamentals (Project Gutenberg #20776). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — modern phrasing of the work-two-together decrease.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decrease worked through the front loops only of two consecutive stitches, then completed as a single stitch. Used in amigurumi to hide the decrease in the fabric — looks like an undecreased stitch from the right side.

heroPrompt: A triangular swatch of treble crochet narrowing from a wide row at the bottom to a single stitch at the top, cream DK cotton, plain background — the angled edges show the decreases on each row.

content.text: A crochet decrease takes two stitches at the base and works them as a single stitch at the top. You start the first stitch but don't finish it; you start the second stitch into the next position; then you finish both at once. The row loses one stitch in width.

Modern British convention writes the move explicitly: "tr2tog over next 2 sts" for a treble decrease, "dc2tog over next 2 sts" for double crochet. The older abbreviation "dec" is less informative — it doesn't say which stitch height or which position. Stick to the explicit form when reading any modern pattern.

attrs.title: Why decreases look different
attrs.body: A decrease has the height of a single stitch but the width of a single stitch covering the position of two. The top of the decrease shows one V; the base spreads across two stitches. A regular decrease leaves a small bump where the two strands join at the top. An invisible decrease (worked through front loops only) hides the bump — useful in amigurumi where the decrease shouldn't show.

content.text: Yarn over. Insert hook into the next stitch. Yarn over, pull a loop back through the stitch. Yarn over, pull through the first two loops. Three loops remain on the hook — the first stitch is started but not finished.

Yarn over again. Insert hook into the next stitch. Yarn over, pull a loop back. Yarn over, pull through the first two loops. Four loops remain on the hook — the second stitch is also started but not finished.
Yarn over once more. Pull through ALL four loops at once. One loop remains on the hook — the decrease is finished. The row has lost one stitch.

Same principle, shorter stitches. Insert hook into the next stitch, yarn over, pull a loop back. Two loops on the hook. Insert hook into the following stitch, yarn over, pull a loop back. Three loops on the hook. Yarn over and pull through all three. The dc2tog is done.

For amigurumi where the decrease shouldn't show, work the dc2tog through the front loops only of the next two stitches. Insert the hook under the front loop of the next stitch, then under the front loop of the following stitch — TWO front loops on the hook before the yarn-over. Yarn over, pull through those two front loops. Two loops on the hook. Yarn over, pull through both. The decrease disappears into the fabric from the right side.

attrs.heading: When decreases don't look right
attrs.intro: Three common decrease problems and the fix for each.

items.symptom: The decrease leaves a noticeable gap or hole in the fabric
items.cause: On treble decreases, the final pull-through pulled too tight. The top of the decrease is squeezed but the base is loose, so a small hole appears between the two base stitches.
items.fix: Match the tension of the decrease to the surrounding stitches — neither tighter nor looser. On treble decreases, the final pull-through should sit at the same height as the adjacent stitch tops.

items.symptom: The decrease looks bulky compared to the surrounding stitches
items.cause: Standard decreases (both loops worked through) carry two stitch tops compressed into one position.
items.fix: For amigurumi, use the invisible decrease (front-loop only). For larger pieces, this is the natural look of a decrease — block the finished piece and the decrease blends in.

items.symptom: The shape narrows by two stitches per decrease, not one
items.cause: You worked tr2tog over THREE stitches by mistake, or the working position skipped a stitch on its way to the decrease.
items.fix: tr2tog uses exactly two consecutive stitches. Count the base stitches under each decrease — two trebles below, one decrease above.

content.text: Pair decreases with increases and the full shaping toolkit opens — a beanie crown decreases six per round to close, a sleeve cap decreases at both edges of every row, an amigurumi animal closes with rounds of decreases at the top. The standard six-per-round decrease in double crochet matches the six-per-round increase in flat-circle work; the same maths, inverted.
